summary.text: The counterexample is \(n=51\), for which \(51\equiv1\pmod 5\) and \(138n+6=7044\). Modular reduction gives \(2^{7044}+2\equiv672\pmod{1398}\), while \(2^{1398}\equiv1\pmod{1399}\) and \(2^{672}+3\equiv0\pmod{1399}\); hence \(1399\) divides the relevant number, so its smallest prime factor is at most \(1399<1669\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
M_k=2^{\,2^k+2}+3,
\]
so that \(a(k)\) is the smallest prime factor of \(M_k\). We disprove the claimed universal statement by taking
\[
n=51.
\]
This value satisfies the conjecture's hypothesis, since
\[
51\equiv 1\pmod 5,
\]
and in particular \(51\not\equiv2\pmod5\). The corresponding sequence index is
\[
138n+6=138\cdot51+6=7038+6=7044.
\]
We will prove that \(1399\) divides
\[
M_{7044}=2^{\,2^{7044}+2}+3.
\]
Since \(1399<1669\), this will force the smallest prime factor of \(M_{7044}\) to be less than \(1669\), contradicting the conjectured value.

We first reduce the exponent \(2^{7044}+2\) modulo \(1398\). Repeated squaring modulo \(1398\) gives the following table. In the row indexed by \(j\), the last entry is the residue of \(2^{2^j}\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
j&2^j&2^{2^j}\pmod{1398}\\ \hline
0&1&2\\
1&2&4\\
2&4&16\\
3&8&256\\
4&16&1228\\
5&32&940\\
6&64&64\\
7&128&1300\\
8&256&1216\\
9&512&970\\
10&1024&46\\
11&2048&718\\
12&4096&1060
\end{array}
\]
Each entry after the first is obtained by squaring the preceding residue and taking the remainder modulo \(1398\), so this table is a direct finite modular calculation.

Now
\[
7044=4096+2048+512+256+128+4.
\]
Consequently, using the appropriate entries from the table and multiplying modulo \(1398\), the successive accumulated residues are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{factor included}&\text{accumulated residue modulo }1398\\ \hline
2^4&16\\
2^4\,2^{128}&16\cdot1300\equiv1228\\
2^4\,2^{128}\,2^{256}&1228\cdot1216\equiv184\\
2^4\,2^{128}\,2^{256}\,2^{512}&184\cdot970\equiv934\\
2^4\,2^{128}\,2^{256}\,2^{512}\,2^{2048}&934\cdot718\equiv970\\
2^4\,2^{128}\,2^{256}\,2^{512}\,2^{2048}\,2^{4096}&970\cdot1060\equiv670.
\end{array}
\]
The product in the final row is \(2^{7044}\). Hence
\[
2^{7044}\equiv670\pmod{1398},
\]
and therefore
\[
2^{7044}+2\equiv672\pmod{1398}.
\]
Equivalently, there is a nonnegative integer \(q\) such that
\[
2^{7044}+2=1398q+672.
\]

We next perform the modular computations needed modulo \(1399\). Repeated squaring of \(2\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
j&2^j&2^{2^j}\pmod{1399}\\ \hline
0&1&2\\
1&2&4\\
2&4&16\\
3&8&256\\
4&16&1182\\
5&32&922\\
6&64&891\\
7&128&648\\
8&256&204\\
9&512&1045\\
10&1024&805.
\end{array}
\]
Again, every residue is obtained by squaring the one immediately above it and reducing modulo \(1399\).

Since
\[
1398=1024+256+64+32+16+4+2,
\]
the table yields \(2^{1398}\) by multiplying the residues belonging to those seven powers of two. The successive products modulo \(1399\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
1\cdot4&\equiv4,\\
4\cdot16&\equiv64,\\
64\cdot1182&\equiv102,\\
102\cdot922&\equiv311,\\
311\cdot891&\equiv99,\\
99\cdot204&\equiv610,\\
610\cdot805&\equiv1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
2^{1398}\equiv1\pmod{1399}.
\]
We also have
\[
672=512+128+32.
\]
Using the entries for exponents \(512,128,32\), respectively, gives
\[
2^{672}\equiv1045\cdot648\cdot922\pmod{1399}.
\]
For example, multiplying in the reverse order, the accumulated residues are
\[
922\cdot648\equiv83\pmod{1399}
\]
and
\[
83\cdot1045\equiv1396\pmod{1399}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{672}\equiv1396\equiv-3\pmod{1399}.
\]

Combining these facts with \(2^{7044}+2=1398q+672\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{\,2^{7044}+2}
  &=2^{1398q+672}\\
  &=(2^{1398})^q2^{672}\\
  &\equiv1^q(-3)\\
  &\equiv-3\pmod{1399}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
M_{7044}=2^{\,2^{7044}+2}+3\equiv0\pmod{1399}.
\]
Thus \(1399\mid M_{7044}\).

For completeness, if an integer \(M>1\) has a divisor \(d>1\), then its smallest prime factor is at most \(d\): indeed, \(d\) itself has a prime divisor \(p\), and then \(p\mid d\mid M\), while \(p\le d\). Applying this with \(M=M_{7044}\) and \(d=1399\) shows
\[
a(7044)\le1399.
\]
Because
\[
1399<1669,
\]
we conclude that
\[
a(7044)\ne1669.
\]
But \(7044=138\cdot51+6\), and \(51\not\equiv2\pmod5\). Hence \(n=51\) satisfies every hypothesis of the conjecture while its asserted conclusion fails. Therefore the conjecture
\[
\forall n\ge0,\quad n\not\equiv2\pmod5\Longrightarrow a(138n+6)=1669
\]
is false.
